plot.actor: Person C — credit coordinator who cleared the Enserco volume and now conceals the breach
plot.victim: Person D — trading desk liaison who relies on credit clearance to decide whether to book further deals
plot.casting_note: Person C is the direct credit and legal coordinator who reports to both Person B and Person D, making her the natural gatekeeper who would have run the credit numbers on Enserco's line volume; Person D is her immediate supervisor on the trading side and the one who must decide whether to accept new Enserco transactions — exactly the person who would rely on a clean credit signal.
plot.true_fact: Enserco Energy has already exceeded its approved credit limit: the surge in online trading volume that Person B flagged on April 20 pushed Enserco's aggregate exposure past the approved ceiling before any new ISDA was in place, and Person C knew this when she processed the most recent batch of trades.
plot.false_belief: Person D believes Enserco is still within its approved credit limit — that the concern raised by Person B is about future risk and growing exposure trending toward the limit, not a limit already breached — and therefore treats the situation as a forward-looking caution rather than an immediate stop.
plot.plot:
The sequence begins two days before Person B's April 20 email reaches Person D.

Person C has been running the daily credit exposure reports for Enserco Energy. The counterparty has been unusually active on the online trading platform — larger lots, more frequent tickets — and sometime on April 18 the cumulative mark-to-market exposure, net of the letters of credit posted as collateral, crosses the approved credit ceiling. Person C sees the number. She knows what it means: any trade booked after that crossing point was technically unauthorized, and at least three tickets went through after the line turned red because she did not halt the queue. Stopping them in real time would have required an immediate call to the trading desk, an explanation, and almost certainly an unwind — a messy, relationship-damaging reversal that would have landed on her desk to administer and on her record as the person who let it get that far.

So Person C does not halt the queue. She notes in her internal workbook that the exposure is 'approaching limit / collateral review pending' — language that is technically accurate about the direction of travel but obscures the fact that the limit has already been passed. She does not send the routine over-limit alert that her own team's procedures require.

On the morning of April 19, Person D sends Person C a short internal message asking for a status check on Enserco ahead of a call with the trading desk: 'Can you confirm Enserco headroom — desk wants to know if we can keep taking their volume through end of month.'

This is the concealment moment.

Person C replies the same morning. Her message reads: 'Enserco exposure is currently sitting at $4.2M net of L/C collateral against a $5M approved limit — so we have room, though the pace of their online volume means we should watch it closely. No hard stop at this point; I'd flag it as a caution rather than a block. The bigger issue is the unsigned ISDA, which Person B is chasing. Once that's executed we can revisit the limit itself if the desk wants to grow the relationship.'

Every number in that message is chosen carefully. The $4.2M figure is the exposure as of the close of April 17 — the last clean snapshot before the line crossed. Person C does not use the April 18 close, which would show $5.3M. She does not say the limit has been breached. She frames the situation as headroom still existing, the ISDA as the primary concern, and the credit position as a 'caution.' A reader of that one message — including Person D — would have no reason to believe anything other than that Enserco is inside its limit and the desk can continue booking, subject to the ISDA caveat.

Person D reads the reply, notes the $4.2M figure against the $5M ceiling, and concludes that there is roughly $800,000 of remaining headroom. He relays this to the trading desk in a brief verbal update: Enserco has room to run through end of month, watch the ISDA situation, no credit stop in place.

The trading desk books two more Enserco tickets that afternoon.

The following day, April 20, Person B's email arrives — the one that will eventually surface the problem. Person B has spoken directly to Enserco's credit manager, Don Perkins, and has independently concluded that no further volume should be taken on until the ISDA is signed. Person B's email to Person D says the exposure is 'increasing due to the size of the online volume' and recommends a halt.

Person D reads Person B's email and is puzzled rather than alarmed. His mental model, built on Person C's April 19 reply, is that Enserco is inside its limit. He interprets Person B's concern as a forward-looking, relationship-management caution — sensible, but not a crisis. He forwards Person B's email to the relevant trading platform contacts as instructed, adding his own note: 'FYI — credit and legal are flagging the ISDA gap as the key issue; exposure is being monitored and is within approved parameters at this stage. Desk should hold off on new Enserco volume pending ISDA execution, but no unwind required on existing book.'

That last clause — 'no unwind required on existing book' — is the reliance moment. Person D is acting on the false belief Person C planted: that the existing trades are fine, that the limit has not been breached, that the only outstanding issue is the unsigned ISDA. He tells the trading desk to pause new business but explicitly reassures them that what is already on the books is clean. No one calls for a review of the April 18 and April 19 tickets. No one asks Person C to produce the daily exposure run for those dates. The trades that crossed the limit stay on the books, unexamined, because the person who would have ordered the review has been told, in specific dollar terms, by the person who ran the numbers, that there is nothing to review.

plot.actor: Person C — regulatory-affairs coordinator who controls the authorization files
plot.victim: Person E — information hub who relies on Person C's status reports to greenlight trading activity
plot.casting_note: Person C is the direct legal and credit coordinator who owns the due-diligence files on each utility and reports upward to Person E; Person E is the information hub who aggregates regulatory status and passes clearance to the trading desk — exactly the relay point where a concealed lapse would do the most damage.
plot.true_fact: The master agreement and accompanying state regulatory authorization for Clearwater Valley Electric Cooperative — one of the ten utilities counted as 'approved' — lapsed sixty days ago when the opinion letter from the utility's local counsel expired without renewal; the authorization is no longer valid and any derivatives trades executed against it are unsupported.
plot.false_belief: Person E believes, on the strength of Person C's explicit written assurance, that all ten executed master agreements are currently in force and that the trading desk may continue booking transactions against each of them without interruption.
plot.plot:
The scene opens in mid-October 1999, a few days before Person C's email to Person E lands in the inbox. The derivatives trading desk has been running a modest but steady flow of power-swap transactions with ten regulated utilities, each of which has gone through the full due-diligence gauntlet: local counsel hired, state regulatory landscape researched, public-utility-commission orders reviewed, and — where required — an opinion letter obtained from the utility's own counsel confirming that the entity is authorized under its state's law to enter derivatives contracts.

One of those ten utilities is Clearwater Valley Electric Cooperative, a mid-sized regulated distribution company in a state whose public-utility commission had issued a conditional order two years earlier permitting Clearwater Valley to trade financial derivatives, subject to annual renewal of a formal opinion letter from outside counsel. The opinion letter was obtained in 1997, renewed in 1998, and then — quietly, without fanfare — allowed to lapse in August 1999 when Clearwater Valley's outside counsel sent a renewal invoice that went unpaid during a billing dispute between the utility and the law firm. No renewed letter was ever issued. The conditional PUC order, by its own terms, requires the opinion letter to remain current; without it, the authorization is void.

Person C knows this. The lapse surfaced in early September 1999 when Person C pulled the Clearwater Valley file to answer a routine internal question about counterparty limits. The file showed the opinion letter dated August 1998, a one-year instrument, with no successor document. Person C flagged it internally in a handwritten note to herself, confirmed with a brief phone call to the state's local counsel that yes, the authorization would be considered lapsed under the PUC order's plain language, and then — because the trading desk was already running live positions against Clearwater Valley and disclosing the lapse would trigger an immediate halt and a scramble to unwind or suspend those trades — Person C made a decision: she would pursue a quiet renewal without surfacing the gap.

She drafted a letter to Clearwater Valley's counsel requesting an updated opinion. The letter went out September 15th. By October 12th, no response had been received.

Meanwhile, Person E — responding to a question from the trading desk about which utilities were cleared for online derivatives trading — sent Person C the email that becomes the ANCHOR: a direct, slightly exasperated note asking whether the ten executed master agreements really represent ten utilities approved to trade, and what is being done about the thirty to forty still in the pipeline. Person E's question is operational: the desk wants to know its approved counterparty list, and Person E needs a clean answer.

Person C drafts her reply the same afternoon. The reply is the concealment moment.

The email Person C sends to Person E reads, in its operative paragraph: 'To answer your question directly — yes, the ten utilities with executed master agreements are approved and their authorizations are current. The due diligence on each of them has been satisfactorily concluded, including where required the receipt of opinion letters from their counsel confirming authorization to trade derivatives under applicable state law and any relevant PUC orders. You may represent to the desk that those ten counterparties are cleared for trading.' She then pivots to the pipeline question, explaining the tiered process for the thirty to forty utilities still under review, and closes with the note — drawn almost verbatim from the ANCHOR — that the process has in the past revealed circumstances preventing a utility from trading or requiring actions not yet taken, which is why approval is withheld until research is complete.

That closing line is the knowing flourish. Person C is aware, as she writes it, that it describes precisely the situation she is concealing: Clearwater Valley is a utility whose authorization requires an action — renewal of the opinion letter — that has not been taken. She writes the general warning into the email as a kind of inoculation, a way of demonstrating her rigor, while simultaneously asserting in the sentence above it that the ten approved utilities are clean. A reader of that email — including Person E — would have no reason to suspect that the warning applied to any member of the approved group. The warning is framed as a reason why some utilities are still in the pipeline, not as a caveat on the ten already cleared.

Person C does not mention Clearwater Valley by name. She does not mention the lapsed opinion letter. She does not mention the September 15th renewal request or the absence of any response. She states, affirmatively and without qualification, that the ten counterparties' authorizations are current.

That is the concealment: a positive, written, knowing assertion of the false version, delivered in response to a direct question, by the one person in the chain who holds the file and knows the true state.

The reliance follows within forty-eight hours. Person E forwards Person C's reply to the trading desk supervisor — call him the desk lead — with a one-line cover: 'Per legal, all ten executed-agreement counterparties are cleared and current. Proceed.' The desk lead, who has been waiting for exactly this confirmation before booking a new tranche of power swaps with Clearwater Valley scheduled to settle in November, treats the message as the green light it appears to be. He instructs his traders to proceed with the Clearwater Valley transactions. The trades are booked. Confirmations go out. The positions appear on the desk's risk report as fully authorized.

At no point does the desk lead know — because Person E does not know, because Person C did not say — that the authorization underpinning those trades expired in August and has not been renewed. The desk is relying on a status that does not exist. The trades run on the strength of Person C's assurance, and the assurance is false.

plot.actor: Person A — the concealer, contract attorney who filed the wrong version
plot.victim: Person C — the misled party, legal and credit coordinator relying on the file
plot.casting_note: Person A, as the attorney who handled the original ISDA Master filing for the Engage Energy account, controls what version is in the file and knows the discrepancy; Person C, delegated by Person D during maternity leave, must rely on whatever Person A tells her the file contains in order to close out the amendment and guaranty review.
plot.true_fact: The executed ISDA Master Agreement on file for Engage Energy US, L.P. is a superseded draft — an earlier negotiated version that was never the final agreed form — meaning the document actually governing live trades between the firm and Engage Energy is not the version both parties ultimately signed.
plot.false_belief: Person C is led to believe that the ISDA Master Agreement on file is the final, fully negotiated and executed version that both parties agreed to, and that the hand-marked amendment in the file represents agreed changes layered on top of that valid base agreement.
plot.plot:
The sequence begins in late July 2000, a few days before Person D goes on maternity leave. Person D has been managing the Engage Energy ISDA Master file and is aware that the negotiation of both the master agreement and a related amendment has been complicated — there were rounds of comments, a set of hand-marked changes on a printed draft, and an outstanding guaranty from Coastal Corporation that Engage faxed over. Person D has not had time to fully reconcile the file before leaving, and she sends the email that becomes the ANCHOR: she asks Person C to finish the matter and to get an attorney involved if necessary, and she separately flags to Person A (Luke, in the original) that she is still waiting on his review of her comments to the amendment draft.

Person A has a problem he has not disclosed to anyone. Several months earlier, when the ISDA Master negotiation with Engage Energy reached its conclusion, Person A was responsible for ensuring the final executed version of the master agreement was filed in the firm's contract management system. In the rush of closing out several deals simultaneously, Person A filed a draft — specifically the version that had been circulated two rounds before the final — rather than the clean execution copy that both parties actually signed. The final executed copy, bearing both signatures, was returned by Engage Energy's counsel and sat briefly in Person A's email inbox before being misfiled in a general correspondence folder. Person A noticed the error approximately six weeks after the fact, pulled up the two documents side by side, and confirmed that the version in the official file was missing three negotiated carve-outs that the trading desk had specifically requested and that Engage Energy had agreed to in the final round. Person A said nothing. Disclosing the error would require explaining to Person G, Person F, and the trading desk that the document actually governing live positions — positions that had already been booked and were accumulating exposure — was not the agreement anyone believed it to be. The enforceability of the netting provisions, in particular, would be immediately questioned. Person A decided to wait for an opportunity to quietly substitute the correct document.

That opportunity does not come before Person D's maternity leave begins. Instead, Person C emails Person A directly, forwarding Person D's handoff note and asking two specific questions: first, what she should compare the Coastal Corporation Guaranty against to confirm it is acceptable, and second, whether the hand-marked changes on the amendment draft in the file are the agreed changes and whether that is the version the firm should execute.

Person A reads Person C's email and understands immediately what it means. Person C is going into the file. If Person C pulls the master agreement to check the guaranty's conformity or to understand the amendment's relationship to the base document, she may notice that the version on file does not match the amendment's recitals, which reference clause numbers and defined terms from the final negotiated form. Person A composes his reply the same afternoon.

The reply is the concealment. Person A writes, in a tone that is collegial and reassuring — consistent with his habit of blending legal precision with warmth — that the file is in order and that Person C should not worry about the base agreement itself, as it was fully executed and on file. He tells her that the Coastal Corporation Guaranty Engage faxed over should be compared against the firm's standard form guaranty, which he attaches to the email, and he notes that the faxed version looks substantially similar to the firm's form and that any minor deviations are cosmetic. On the amendment, Person A writes: 'The hand-marked copy in the file reflects the agreed changes — those marks were initialed off by both sides during the final call. That is the version we should execute. The underlying Master is clean and in place, so the amendment slots in without issue.' He does not qualify this. He does not say 'I believe' or 'as far as I recall.' He states it as settled fact: the Master is clean and in place. A reader seeing only that sentence would have no reason to doubt it. Person A knows, as he types it, that the Master on file is not clean — it is the wrong draft — and that the amendment, if executed against the file version, will be layered onto a document that does not reflect what the parties actually agreed.

Person C receives Person A's reply and treats it as authoritative. Person A is the attorney of record on the matter; Person D has told her to get an attorney involved if necessary, and here the attorney has already weighed in and confirmed the file is in order. Person C does not pull the master agreement itself to read it. She compares the faxed Coastal Corporation Guaranty against the standard form Person A attached, notes the similarities, and drafts a short memo concluding that the guaranty is acceptable with one minor conforming change. She then prepares a cover letter to Engage Energy's counsel enclosing the amendment for execution, referencing the ISDA Master Agreement on file as the governing document and confirming that the hand-marked changes are the agreed form. She routes the execution package through Person B for sign-off, noting in her routing memo that the underlying Master is confirmed in place by counsel and that the amendment is ready for signature.

Person B, relying on Person C's routing memo and the implicit authority of Person A's review, approves the package for execution. The amendment is sent to Engage Energy. Engage Energy executes and returns it. The trading desk is notified that the ISDA documentation with Engage Energy is fully in order — master agreement in place, amendment executed, guaranty confirmed — and books additional trades against the counterparty with the understanding that the netting and close-out provisions of the final negotiated master agreement protect the firm's positions.

The version of the master agreement actually governing those positions is the superseded draft. The three carve-outs the trading desk negotiated — including a modified cross-default threshold and a revised termination currency provision — do not exist in the document on file. No one on the trading desk knows this. Person C does not know this. Person B does not know this. Person A knows, and Person A's email to Person C — 'The underlying Master is clean and in place' — is the moment the secret is sealed into the transaction record.

topic.name: Force majeure claim already denied
topic.secret: A contract attorney conceals from the trading desk that a counterparty's formal force majeure claim has already been reviewed and rejected by the company, allowing the desk to continue treating delivery obligations as suspended and the counterparty as excused, because admitting the rejection would force the desk to immediately pursue breach remedies and expose that the attorney failed to communicate the denial in time.
topic.either_or: SIDE A: the force majeure claim has been formally rejected and the counterparty remains in breach  vs  SIDE B: the force majeure claim is still under review and the counterparty's obligations are suspended

plot.actor: Person F — contract attorney who controls the force majeure file and conceals the denial
plot.victim: Person G — high-level legal reviewer and executive who relies on Person F's characterisation before advising the trading desk
plot.casting_note: Person F reports to Person G and delegates downward to Person C, making Person F the natural gatekeeper of the force majeure correspondence; Person G is the senior authority to whom Person E escalates the breach question, so Person G is the one who will set the desk's course of action — exactly the person who must be kept in the dark for the concealment to hold
plot.true_fact: The counterparty's formal force majeure claim was reviewed by Person F and formally rejected by the company several days earlier; the counterparty is therefore in active breach of its delivery obligations and the company has the right — and arguably the duty — to pursue breach remedies immediately
plot.false_belief: Person G believes the force majeure claim is still under substantive legal review, that no determination has been made, and that the counterparty's obligations remain suspended pending that review — meaning the trading desk need not yet treat the situation as a breach or pursue remedies
plot.plot:
The sequence begins a few days before the anchor email. Person F, working the contract file for a gas or power delivery agreement, receives a formal written force majeure notice from the counterparty citing an operational disruption. Person F circulates it internally, Person C runs the factual checklist against the contract's force majeure clause, and the conclusion is unambiguous: the claimed event does not satisfy the contractual definition — it is foreseeable, it is within the counterparty's reasonable control, and the notice was delivered outside the contractual window. Person F drafts a rejection letter on behalf of the company, it is signed and transmitted to the counterparty. From that moment the counterparty is in breach. Person F knows this. Person C knows this. The file is closed on the force majeure question; what remains open is what to do about the breach itself.

Person F does not route the rejection letter to the trading desk. Person F does not send it to Person G. Person F does not copy Person B or Person E. The letter sits in the outgoing correspondence log that only Person F and Person C regularly touch. Person F's reasoning — never written down — is that communicating the denial will immediately trigger a demand from the trading desk to issue a default notice, which will in turn expose that Person F sat on the rejection for several days before escalating, a delay that could itself be characterised as a failure of duty. Person F calculates that if the situation can be kept framed as 'still under review,' the desk will continue treating deliveries as suspended, no one will ask why no default notice has gone out, and Person F will have time to construct a cleaner narrative.

On 24 January Person E, who serves as the information hub between the legal team and the trading desk, receives an urgent message from the trading desk — Louise Kitchen's group — flagging that the counterparty has now missed a second scheduled delivery and asking what the legal position is. Person E, who has heard nothing definitive from Person F about the force majeure claim, forwards the question up the chain: the anchor email, Person E to Person G, subject line referencing the contract violation, body reading: 'We need to act on this today — what is your advice on how we proceed based on the fact that they clearly appear to be in breach.'

Person G, receiving this, does not have the force majeure file in front of her. She calls Person F directly, asking for a status summary before she responds to Person E and the desk. This is the concealment moment.

plot.victim: Person H — risk analyst who prices and manages credit derivative exposure
plot.casting_note: Person C is the direct legal and credit coordinator who handled the ISDA/GTC assignment question and would have reviewed the executed agreement; Person H is the regulatory and risk analyst who relies on confirmed contract terms to model counterparty exposure — exactly the desk-side function that would price risk against an assumed indemnity protection.

plot.plot:
The trouble began, as it often did, with an unresolved structural question. Person C had been chasing Person E and Person D for weeks about whether the credit derivatives sitting on the platform should be governed by the applicable ISDA Master Agreement or routed under a General Terms and Conditions contract. The email Person C sent on May 3rd was blunt: no global contract was assigned to any of the credit derivatives online, and it was causing friction between Global Contract and the online crew. Person E had initially assumed everything would go under a GTC, then wavered. Person D had not yet weighed in with a final direction.

While that governance question was still nominally open, a separate but related piece of work had already closed — or so everyone believed. Several weeks earlier, Person C had been responsible for shepherding the final execution of a master trading agreement with a key counterparty, a document that sat beneath the credit derivatives in question and that contained, among its standard protective provisions, an indemnity clause shielding the trading desk from certain categories of counterparty-caused loss. The clause had been negotiated carefully. Person A, working under Person F, had flagged it as material during the drafting phase. Person G had signed off on the term sheet that included it. The trading desk — and specifically Person H, who was responsible for modeling the risk profile of the credit derivative book — had been told the indemnity was in the agreement and had built it into the desk's exposure calculations accordingly.

What Person C had not told anyone was what Person C had discovered three days after the agreement was countersigned and returned: the counterparty's execution copy, the one that now constituted the binding document, was missing the indemnity clause entirely. It had been in the penultimate draft. It was not in the final. Somewhere in the last round of redlines — a round Person C had reviewed and approved for signature — the clause had been deleted. Person C did not know whether the counterparty had stripped it deliberately or whether it had been lost in a formatting error during the clean-copy preparation. What Person C knew was that Person C had signed off on the document without catching the omission, and that the agreement was now executed and binding without the protection the desk believed it had.

Person C said nothing. Not to Person D. Not to Person E. Not to Person F or Person G. Not to Person H.

The concealment became active — not merely passive — on May 9th, six days after the governance email. Person H sent a short message to Person C and Person B, copying Person D, asking for confirmation of the contractual framework before Person H finalized the desk's quarterly risk report. Person H's message was specific: 'Can you confirm the executed master with [counterparty] includes the standard indemnity provision we discussed? I want to make sure I'm reflecting the correct protection level in the exposure model before this goes to senior management.' It was a direct question. It had a binary answer.

Person C replied the same afternoon. The reply was brief, collegial, and precise in its false assurance. Person C wrote: 'Yes — the executed agreement with [counterparty] is in place and contains the indemnity provision. You're fine to rely on it for the report. We're still sorting out the ISDA vs. GTC assignment question for the online platform, but that's a separate matter and doesn't affect the executed master. The protection you've been modeling is there.' Person C did not hedge. Person C did not say 'I believe' or 'to my knowledge.' Person C stated it as settled fact, in the same efficient, authoritative register Person C used for every routine legal confirmation — because that register was precisely what would prevent Person H from asking a follow-up question.

Person H read the reply, noted it, and finalized the quarterly risk report. The report went to Person G and Person I with the counterparty exposure modeled at the reduced risk level that the indemnity clause justified. The credit derivative positions were sized, and the reserve calculations were set, on the premise that a loss event attributable to the counterparty would be partially absorbed by the contractual indemnity. Person H also used the confirmed framework to advise on two new credit derivative trades entered that week, recommending terms that would have been priced differently — with wider spreads, or with additional collateral requirements — had the desk known the indemnity was absent. The trades were executed on Person H's recommendation. The desk was exposed in ways it did not know it was exposed, and it remained so because the one person who knew the agreement's true contents had answered a direct question with the wrong answer and had done so knowing it was wrong.

The margin exception report has been circulating for several days by the time Person D sends the coordinating email on November 10, 1999. The list runs to roughly two dozen counterparties, several of them Canadian, and the internal consensus — shared by Person B, Person D, the trading desk, and Person G at the executive level — is that the team will walk into the review meeting holding every available remedy as a bargaining chip. The most valuable chip on the Canadian side is the outstanding collateral call against Counterparty 7, a mid-size Calgary-based energy trader that missed a variation-margin deadline ten days earlier. The call was issued under the credit-support annex to the ISDA master agreement, and the desk has been treating the counterparty as in technical default ever since. Person B has told the traders explicitly: do not renegotiate the exposure threshold with Counterparty 7 until we see whether they blink on the collateral.

What Person B does not know is that Person C, three days before Person D's email goes out, received a call from Counterparty 7's treasurer. The treasurer argued that the missed margin deadline resulted from a wire-routing error at their custodian bank, not from any credit deterioration, and asked for a written waiver of the specific call so that the default notation would not appear in their regulatory filings. Person C, judging the explanation plausible and wanting to preserve the commercial relationship, drafted a one-paragraph waiver letter on company letterhead, signed it under the authority delegated by Person D and Person B, and transmitted it to the counterparty's back office by fax. The letter stated that the company 'hereby waives, as of November 7, 1999, the collateral call issued on October 31, 1999, and confirms that no event of default is deemed to exist with respect to such call.' Person C filed the fax confirmation in the counterparty credit folder and moved on. Person C did not copy Person B, did not copy the trading desk, and did not update the margin exception list.

The morning after Person D's coordinating email, Person B replies to the thread to ask Person C for a status line on each counterparty before the meeting — specifically whether each call is 'still open and enforceable or resolved.' Person C responds the same afternoon. The reply is a bulleted list, counterparty by counterparty. Next to Counterparty 7, Person C writes: 'Call issued 10/31, no posting received to date, default position preserved — recommend we hold firm on threshold renegotiation until they perform.' Person C does not write that the call has been waived. Person C writes the opposite: that the default position is preserved and that the desk should hold firm. A reader seeing only that bullet point would understand it as a status report from the person who controls the credit file — an affirmative representation that the call is live. Person C knows, at the moment of writing, that the waiver letter has already been transmitted and accepted. The bullet point is not an omission; it is a characterization of the counterparty's status that Person C knows to be false.

Person B reads the list, notes that Counterparty 7 is still in the 'hold firm' column, and incorporates that into the meeting preparation. The night before the review session, Person B drafts a one-page talking-points memo for Person G summarizing the team's leverage positions. Under the Canadian counterparties section, Person B writes: 'Counterparty 7 — collateral call outstanding since 10/31, no cure, technical default intact; we are positioned to condition any threshold amendment on immediate full posting or a credit-enhancement substitute.' The counterparty's representative pauses, then says she will need to check with her back office, because she understood the matter had been closed. The trading desk lead, puzzled, looks across the table at Person B. Person B looks at Person C. Person C says nothing.

plot.victim: Person C — the legal and credit coordinator who relies on the agreement's authorized status to direct the trading desk

The trouble with TDCC had been building since early 1999. Person E's February 2001 email to Person C laid it out plainly: two years earlier, credit negotiations had collapsed because TDCC refused to sign any master agreement containing credit terms at all. Rod Nelson in Credit had been the responsible officer at the time; the deal had simply died. Now TDCC was back, and their message was unambiguous — they had never accepted the terms and conditions embedded in the firm's confirmations, and they could not accept them. Person E's instruction was equally unambiguous: derivatives trading with TDCC should stop immediately on legal grounds until the matter was resolved, and the first step toward any new master agreement had to be a fresh approach to Credit to generate proper credit terms.

Person C received that email and forwarded it up the chain to Person B, flagging it as urgent. Person B, in turn, tasked Person A — the contract attorney assigned to derivatives documentation — with reviewing the TDCC file and reporting back on the current state of the master agreement before any decision about resuming or halting trading could be made.

Person A knew exactly what the file contained. In late 2000, under pressure from the trading desk to get TDCC trades documented before year-end, Person A had drafted a modified ISDA master that stripped out the standard credit-support annex — the very terms TDCC had always refused — and had circulated it to TDCC's counsel. TDCC had countersigned. Person A had filed the executed agreement and had notified the trading desk that a master was in place. What Person A had not done — and what the firm's derivatives documentation policy explicitly required for any master agreement that deviated from the standard credit template — was submit the agreement to the internal credit committee for approval, or escalate it to the board-level derivatives authorization panel. The policy existed precisely because stripping credit terms from a master agreement was a material risk decision, not a documentation decision. Person A had known this at the time. The submission would have required Person A to explain why the credit annex had been removed, which would have surfaced the fact that TDCC's refusal to accept any credit terms had been the reason the 1999 negotiations failed — and that the firm was now proposing to trade with TDCC on an unsecured basis. Person A had judged, privately, that the committee would either reject the agreement or delay it past the trading desk's year-end deadline. So Person A had executed it and said nothing about the approval step.

Now, in February 2001, Person B was asking for a status report.

Person A composed a reply to Person B, copied to Person C, that read in its operative paragraph: 'I have reviewed the TDCC master agreement file. The modified ISDA master with TDCC was executed in November 2000 and the agreement is on file. The credit-support annex was negotiated out at TDCC's insistence, which is consistent with the history Person E describes from 1999, but the agreement itself went through the firm's internal review process and authorization is documented. The trading desk has been booking against it since Q4 2000. Given Person E's note about TDCC's position on confirmations, the more pressing issue is whether TDCC's back office is properly processing those confirmations — that is a separate operational matter from the master's validity. The master is valid and authorized.'

That sentence — 'the agreement itself went through the firm's internal review process and authorization is documented' — was the concealment. It was not an omission or a hedge. It was a declarative statement of a fact that Person A knew to be false. There was no internal review. There was no authorization. There was no documentation of approval, because no approval had ever been sought. Person A wrote it in the same flat, administrative register used for routine status updates, sandwiched between accurate observations about TDCC's confirmation practices, so that a reader — including Person C — would absorb it as a settled, already-verified background fact rather than a claim requiring scrutiny.

Person C read the email. Person C's role was coordination, not independent legal audit; Person A was the attorney of record on the TDCC file, and Person A had just confirmed that the master was authorized and on file. Person C drafted a response to Person E and Person B that same afternoon: 'Per Person A's review, the TDCC master agreement executed in November 2000 is valid and authorized. The immediate issue flagged by Person E regarding confirmation acceptance appears to be an operational matter on TDCC's end rather than a defect in the master. I am recommending to the trading desk that they continue booking under the existing master while we address the confirmation processing issue separately with TDCC's back office. I will coordinate with Credit on the confirmation question.'

Person C then sent a separate, brief message to the trading desk supervisor: 'The TDCC ISDA master is confirmed authorized and on file. You are clear to continue booking trades against it. Legal is handling the confirmation issue on the back-office side.'

The trading desk, receiving that clearance from Person C — who had received it from Person A — continued to book. New TDCC trades were entered into the system that week. Existing positions, which might have been frozen pending a legal review, remained open and active. The trading desk had no reason to ask whether a credit committee had ever seen the agreement, because Person C had told them it was authorized, and Person C believed that because Person A had said authorization was documented.

The missing approval — the one that would have required a senior credit officer and a board-level panel to sign off on an unsecured master agreement with a counterparty that had a documented history of refusing credit terms — did not exist anywhere in the firm's records. It had never been sought. Person A was the only person in the chain who knew this, and Person A had just told the chain the opposite.

plot.false_belief: Person G believes the right to demand arbitration remains live and available, and continues to use the threat of arbitration as leverage in ongoing dispute negotiations with the counterparty
plot.plot:
The dispute with the online counterparty had been simmering for weeks before the arbitration-language review landed on Person G's desk. The counterparty had insisted, in its proposed Online Agreement language, that only monetary damages could be awarded in any arbitration proceeding and that specific performance was categorically unavailable as a remedy against them. Person G forwarded that language to Person D with a pointed note — 'Please take a look at point #6' — because the trading desk needed to know whether to push back hard or accept the limitation. What Person G did not know, and what Person F had been quietly managing around, was that the window to actually demand arbitration had already closed.

The deadline had been buried in the original master agreement with the counterparty — a rolling 90-day trigger from the date the disputed transaction settled. Person F had flagged it internally to Person C in early April, asking Person C to calendar a response date and prepare a demand. Person C had drafted a preliminary demand letter and sent it to Person F for sign-off. Person F had held it, waiting for one more round of commercial negotiations to conclude, reasoning that filing a formal demand might harden the counterparty's position. The commercial talks dragged. The 90-day window closed on April 28. No demand was filed.

By May 5, when Person D's forwarded chain reached Person G, Person F knew the deadline had lapsed. Person F also knew that Person G was about to weigh in on the arbitration-language negotiation — the very negotiation whose entire premise was that arbitration remained a tool the trading desk could deploy.

Person F did not correct the record. Instead, on the morning of May 5, Person F sent Person G the following:

'G — I've reviewed the counterparty's proposed arbitration language at point #6. The restriction to monetary damages only, with specific performance carved out, is a significant concession for us to make, and I would not recommend accepting it as drafted. Our arbitration right under the master agreement is intact and gives us meaningful leverage here. I'd push back and insist on preserving the full remedial menu — including specific performance — before we agree to any revised Online Agreement language. We are in a strong procedural posture to do so. Let me know if you want me to draft the counter-language. — F'

That paragraph — 'Our arbitration right under the master agreement is intact and gives us meaningful leverage here' and 'We are in a strong procedural posture to do so' — was the concealment. Person F stated, as a current and affirmative fact, that the arbitration right was intact. Person F knew it was not. The phrase 'strong procedural posture' was a knowing misdirection: the only procedural reality was that the right had expired four days earlier. A reader of that message, seeing it in isolation, would have no reason to doubt that counsel had just confirmed the remedy was available. Person F did not hedge, did not qualify, did not say 'subject to confirming our demand deadline.' Person F said 'intact' and 'strong.'

Person G read the message and acted on it the same afternoon. Person G drafted a response to the counterparty's negotiating team — routed through Person D and Person B for coordination — stating that the trading desk could not accept the limitation to monetary damages only, that the company reserved its full arbitration rights including the right to seek specific performance, and that if the counterparty insisted on the carve-out the company was prepared to invoke those rights formally rather than continue negotiating. The letter was framed as a credible threat precisely because Person G believed, on the strength of Person F's assurance, that the threat was real.

The trading desk, receiving a summary of Person G's position through Person E's coordination channel, updated its internal dispute tracker to show arbitration as a 'live option, counsel confirms available,' and adjusted its settlement floor accordingly — holding out for better commercial terms because the team believed it had a procedural hammer it could bring down if talks failed.

The hammer did not exist. It had ceased to exist on April 28. Person F's email of May 5 had simply ensured that no one at the table knew that.

plot.plot:
The trouble begins three days before the anchor email is sent. A formal written notice arrives in Person E's inbox from the Canadian energy price-reporting body that publishes the [firm] Daily Index. The notice is unambiguous: effective the first of the month, the index series cited by name in the firm's Canadian trading master agreements is declared discontinued and is no longer a valid contractual reference for settlement or pricing purposes. The publishing body instructs all counterparties to transition to a successor methodology or negotiate alternative fallback language before any further trades are priced against the old series. Person E reads the notice twice, saves it to a subfolder, and does not forward it to anyone.

Her reason, reconstructed from what she does next, is straightforward and self-protective: she had been the attorney who reviewed and approved the master agreement language six months earlier. She had seen an earlier industry consultation document hinting that the index was under review, had noted it internally as something to monitor, and had then let it slip. If she surfaces the discontinuation notice now, the first question from Person G or Person F will be when she received the earlier consultation and why she did not flag it then. The renegotiation that would follow — fallback rate, spread adjustment, retroactive settlement review — would make her omission impossible to hide. So she files the notice and says nothing.

On the morning of February 14, 2001, Person B sends Person E a short internal message asking for a status update on the Canadian trading platform product before the afternoon call with the trading desk. The desk needs to know whether to proceed with pricing the first batch of Canadian trades under the master agreement's index reference, and Person B wants to give them a clean answer. She asks specifically: 'Is the Daily Index reference in the master agreement still the right one to use, or do we have any open issues on the index itself beyond the holiday language you mentioned?'

Person E replies within twenty minutes. Her reply is the concealment moment. She writes: 'The index reference is fine — that's not one of our open items. The two issues I flagged to Greg are the only ones: the holiday-language redundancy, which is a clean drafting fix, and the CFTC scrutiny question on price discovery, which I expect to resolve this afternoon once I hear back from CFTC counsel. On the index itself, we're good. The [firm] Daily Index is the correct and operative reference under the master agreement and I see no issue there. Once we get the CFTC answer we should be in a position to tell the desk to proceed.' She does not hedge. She does not say the index question is under review. She states, as a present and settled fact, that the index is correct and operative. A reader seeing only that reply would have no reason to doubt it; it reads as the considered view of the attorney who knows the file.

Person B, satisfied, forwards Person E's characterization to Person C and Person D with a brief instruction: 'Per Person E, the index reference is confirmed good. The open items are the holiday language and the CFTC question, both in progress. Please let the trading desk know they can treat the [firm] Daily Index as the valid settlement reference and begin preparing the first trade confirmations accordingly. We'll send a final green light once the CFTC answer comes in, but the index itself is not a blocker.'

That afternoon, Person C relays the message to the trading desk. The desk, relying on the legal team's confirmation, prices and books the first three Canadian trades using the [firm] Daily Index as the contractual settlement reference — the same index the publishing body has already declared discontinued. The confirmations go out to counterparties citing the discontinued series by name. The fallback rate that would have applied under a properly renegotiated agreement — a successor index trading at a modest but non-trivial spread to the old series — is never discussed. The desk has no reason to ask; they have been told by the coordinator who was told by the attorney that the index is the correct and operative reference.

The CFTC answer arrives that same afternoon, as Person E predicted, and it is cautiously favorable on the regulatory question. Person E sends a follow-up to Person B: 'CFTC counsel comfortable with the Canadian product as structured, given it's a Canadian price and [firm] is always a party. We're clear to proceed. I'll finalize the holiday language fix and circulate a clean draft tomorrow.' Person B forwards this to the desk as the final green light. More trades are booked.

The discontinued index continues to be used as the settlement reference for weeks. Each day the desk pulls the old series' last published value — the publishing body has left historical data accessible even after the discontinuation — and prices against it, not knowing that the contractual authority for doing so has been formally extinguished. Person E knows. She receives a second, follow-up notice from the publishing body in early March reminding counterparties of the transition deadline. She saves that one too.

The background is the summer of 2000. The company is locked in a contract dispute with TVA. TVA has sued for specific performance, demanding the company honor a long-term power supply agreement. The company's litigation team has been telling the trading desk — and the executives above them — that the case is defensible, that TVA's specific-performance theory has real vulnerabilities, and that TVA will likely accept a negotiated settlement rather than risk a full trial. The pillar holding up that assessment is a witness statement from a former TVA counterparty manager who, in a sworn declaration taken the previous autumn, described TVA's own internal communications as inconsistent with the contract terms TVA was now trying to enforce. That declaration has been the company's best piece of evidence.

What Person F knows, and has known for eleven days, is that the witness has recanted. The recantation is formal: a signed letter to opposing counsel, copied to the court, stating that the declarant reviewed the original statement with independent counsel, concluded it was incomplete and misleading in material respects, and withdraws it in its entirety. Outside counsel — Bob — flagged this to Person F in a phone call on June 30th and followed up with a written summary on July 2nd. Bob's summary is blunt: without that declaration, the company's argument that TVA cannot reasonably demand cover for the entire contract period loses its factual anchor. Bob's view, already communicated to Person F verbally, is that the recantation shifts the balance of the case and that the company should reconsider whether its settlement offers are calibrated to a realistic assessment of litigation risk.

Person F has not passed any of this to Person G.

Instead, on July 11th, Person F sends Person G the draft TVA memo — the ANCHOR email. The memo is framed as a strategic puzzle about deal structure: should the company propose a two-year supply arrangement or a seven-year one? Person F writes that the benefit of a seven-year proposal is uncertain because TVA's specific-performance posture may mean TVA has no obligation to cover the entire period — and Person F attributes this uncertainty to what 'our outside counsel has said in the past,' noting that Bob has explained TVA's specific-performance claim may make full-period cover unreasonable. Person F flags this as an open question about deal mechanics, something to be resolved by talking to Bob that evening.

That framing is the concealment. Person F is presenting the legal uncertainty as a forward-looking structural question — how do we cap our damages if TVA accepts a proposal and we still lose the termination argument? — when the real reason the damages calculus has changed is the recantation of the witness statement. By writing 'according to Bob, since TVA is asking for specific performance, it may not be reasonable for TVA to cover entire period,' Person F is accurately quoting Bob's legal theory but stripping away the reason Bob's assessment of the company's position has darkened: the evidentiary foundation that made the company's termination argument credible is gone. The memo reads as a counsel wrestling with deal-structure nuance. It does not read — and is not written to read — as a counsel disclosing that the case has materially weakened. A reader of that email sees a lawyer doing careful scenario analysis. They do not see a lawyer who is sitting on a recantation letter.

Person F closes the memo by saying: 'Let me know what you think. I'll be in early tomorrow.' The tone is collegial and routine. There is no flag, no asterisk, no 'there is something else you need to know before we finalize this.' The memo is marked confidential and attorney-client privileged, which ensures it will not circulate beyond Person G without Person F's knowledge.

Person G reads the memo that evening. Person G's read is exactly what Person F's framing invites: this is a structuring problem. The company's legal position is intact; the question is whether a seven-year proposal actually caps damages or whether the specific-performance theory TVA is running means the cap is illusory regardless of term length. Person G responds the next morning, before Person F arrives, with a short reply: the two-year proposal is probably cleaner precisely because the seven-year structure does not appear to provide the cap benefit they had hoped for, and the company's strong underlying position on the termination argument means they do not need to over-engineer the settlement offer. Person G adds that Person F should finalize the memo to Delainey along those lines and that the trading desk should be told the company's posture remains firm — TVA is unlikely to take this to judgment given the evidentiary record, and the desk should model the scenario where TVA accepts the company's terms within the next sixty days.

That instruction to the trading desk is the reliance. Person G, having read Person F's memo and seen nothing that disturbed the picture of a company with a strong evidentiary record, directs the desk to continue pricing and hedging on the assumption that TVA will settle favorably. The desk does not mark down the litigation risk. The desk does not reserve against an adverse judgment. The desk continues to treat the company's exposure as bounded and manageable, because the senior legal reviewer has just confirmed, on the basis of Person F's memo, that the evidentiary record is sound.

The witness statement is not sound. It no longer exists as a piece of evidence. The company is litigating on a foundation that has already been pulled out, and the trading desk is making real commercial decisions — on supply commitments, on hedge ratios, on how aggressively to negotiate with TVA — on the basis of a legal strength that Person F knows is no longer there. Person F will talk to Bob that evening, as promised, but the conversation will be about deal structure, not disclosure. The recantation letter sits in Person F's files, marked privileged, and the memo to Delainey will go out in the morning without mentioning it.

For several weeks the picture had looked genuinely promising. Outside counsel had located a former Enerdata data analyst — call him the Witness — who had been present in the room when NGX's representatives arrived with the two-days'-notice demand. The Witness had provided a detailed sworn statement describing the meeting as explicitly coercive: NGX's representative had said, in words the Witness recalled clearly, that Enerdata's index publication business would 'find itself without a data source' if it did not cooperate. That statement, filed in the proceedings, was the hinge on which the company's entire theory of liability turned. Without it, the case rested on circumstantial timing and commercial inference. With it, the case had a human voice, a specific room, a specific threat.

Person F had summarized the Witness's statement in an internal memorandum circulated to Person G, Person H, and Person I in late February, describing the company's position as 'well-supported by direct testimonial evidence' and noting that outside counsel assessed settlement probability at above seventy percent on terms favorable to the company. Person H had taken that memorandum, run it through the risk framework, and recommended to Person I that the trading desk reduce its hedge on the index-linked contracts — the legal cushion, in Person H's analysis, was doing enough work that the financial hedge was redundant and costly.

The recantation arrived in outside counsel's inbox on a Tuesday in the third week of March. The Witness, through his own newly retained lawyer, had submitted a formal written withdrawal of his prior statement. The withdrawal was careful and complete: the Witness stated that he had overstated his certainty about the specific words used, that he could not in good conscience maintain the statement as sworn, and that he was retracting it in its entirety. Outside counsel called Person F the same afternoon. Person F listened, asked three clarifying questions, confirmed that the withdrawal was formal and on the record, and then sat with the information for the remainder of the day.

The problem Person F faced was not merely tactical. Person F had, over the preceding six weeks, been the author of every internal update describing the case as strong. Person G had relied on those updates in a call with senior management. Person H had moved the risk numbers. Person I had signed off on the hedge reduction. If Person F now disclosed the recantation accurately — witness gone, case materially weakened, settlement probability revised sharply downward — the immediate question from every direction would be: when did you know, and why did the internal updates not reflect the deteriorating witness situation earlier? Person F had, in fact, received a preliminary signal from outside counsel two weeks prior that the Witness was 'expressing reservations' and had chosen to characterize that in an internal note as 'routine pre-trial nerves, no impact on the statement's admissibility.' That note was still on the file. A full disclosure now would require Person F to explain that note, and the explanation would not be comfortable.

Person F composed the update email to Person H on Wednesday morning. The subject line read: 'NGX/Enerdata — Litigation Status Update (March).' The body of the email ran four paragraphs. The first recapped the procedural posture — discovery ongoing, outside counsel engaged, next case management conference scheduled. The second described the index-methodology arguments as 'continuing to develop favorably,' noting that the documentary record of the two-days'-notice demand remained 'uncontested by the opposing party.' The third paragraph was the concealment: 'Outside counsel has completed its review of the evidentiary record and confirms that the witness evidence supporting our position remains on file and available for the proceedings. There is no change to the assessment of the testimonial support for our case. Outside counsel's view of settlement probability is unchanged.' The fourth paragraph noted upcoming deadlines and asked Person H to flag any questions to Person C for coordination.

Every sentence in the third paragraph was, in isolation, technically navigable — 'remains on file' was true in the narrow sense that the original statement had not been physically removed from the court file, only formally withdrawn by the witness himself; 'available for the proceedings' was ambiguous enough to mean anything; 'no change to the assessment' was a flat lie dressed as a status report. But the paragraph was not written to be parsed in isolation. It was written to be read by Person H as a routine confirmation that nothing had changed. And it worked exactly as intended.

Person H read the update that Wednesday afternoon between two other coordination calls. The third paragraph registered as a green light — outside counsel had reviewed everything, the witness evidence was solid, settlement probability held. Person H forwarded the update to Person I with a one-line note: 'Legal confirms no change to position strength — our risk reserve assumptions for the NGX contracts remain valid, no adjustment needed this quarter.' Person I acknowledged with a brief reply and closed the loop with the trading desk: the hedge reduction that Person H had recommended the previous month would stand, and the desk's open index-linked positions would continue to be carried at the valuation that assumed a favorable settlement was the most probable outcome.

The trading desk, reading the risk posture as stable, did not reprice the counterparty exposure. The contracts that turned on the NGX-recalculated indices — the ones Person G's original January email had described as 'hundreds of our trading contracts and thousands of transactions' — continued to be marked on the assumption that the legal dispute would resolve in the company's favor and that the index methodology change would ultimately be found to have been coercive and therefore void. The financial consequence of that assumption was not trivial: it was the difference between carrying those positions as near-par and carrying them at a discount that reflected genuine litigation risk.

Person F, meanwhile, sent a separate note to outside counsel the same Wednesday, asking them to 'continue exploring whether the recantation can be challenged or whether a supplementary witness can be identified,' and instructing them not to file any formal notice of the withdrawal with the court until that exploration was complete — a delay that was itself procedurally questionable but bought additional time before the recantation became visible in the public record. Outside counsel acknowledged. The file moved forward. Person H's risk numbers held. The trading desk remained exposed. And the third paragraph of the Wednesday update sat in Person H's inbox, doing exactly the work Person F had needed it to do.
